claim: Malaria parasites use the RhopH complex for erythrocyte invasion and channel-mediated nutrient uptake.
source: Malaria parasites use the RhopH complex for erythrocyte invasion and channel-mediated nutrient uptake.
evidence: This is stated in the title and abstract as the main finding of the study.

claim: The RhopH complex member proteins are unique to Plasmodium spp.
source: As the member proteins are unique to Plasmodium spp., how they interact and traffic through subcellular sites to serve these essential functions is unknown.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as established knowledge about the RhopH complex.

claim: RhopH is synthesized as a soluble complex of CLAG3, RhopH2, and RhopH3 with 1:1:1 stoichiometry.
source: We show that RhopH is synthesized as a soluble complex of CLAG3, RhopH2, and RhopH3 with 1:1:1 stoichiometry.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1E.

claim: After transfer to a new host cell, the RhopH complex crosses a vacuolar membrane surrounding the intracellular parasite.
source: After transfer to a new host cell, the complex crosses a vacuolar membrane surrounding the intracellular parasite and becomes integral to the erythrocyte membrane through a PTEX translocon-dependent process.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by fractionation studies in Figure 4.

claim: The RhopH complex becomes integral to the erythrocyte membrane through a PTEX translocon-dependent process.
source: After transfer to a new host cell, the complex crosses a vacuolar membrane surrounding the intracellular parasite and becomes integral to the erythrocyte membrane through a PTEX translocon-dependent process.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by PTEX knockdown experiments in Figure 4F.

claim: The structure of the trafficking RhopH complex was determined at 2.9 Å resolution using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy.
source: We present a 2.9 Å single-particle cryo-electron microscopy structure of the trafficking complex, revealing that CLAG3 interacts with the other subunits over large surface areas.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and detailed in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: CLAG3 interacts with the other RhopH subunits over large surface areas.
source: We present a 2.9 Å single-particle cryo-electron microscopy structure of the trafficking complex, revealing that CLAG3 interacts with the other subunits over large surface areas.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: The soluble RhopH complex is tightly assembled with extensive disulfide bonding.
source: This soluble complex is tightly assembled with extensive disulfide bonding and predicted transmembrane helices shielded.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Predicted transmembrane helices are shielded in the soluble RhopH complex.
source: This soluble complex is tightly assembled with extensive disulfide bonding and predicted transmembrane helices shielded.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The RhopH complex undergoes large-scale rearrangements for host membrane insertion.
source: We propose a large protein complex stabilized for trafficking but poised for host membrane insertion through large-scale rearrangements, paralleling smaller two-state pore-forming proteins in other organisms.
evidence: This is proposed in the abstract based on structural features and comparison to other pore-forming proteins.

claim: Malaria parasites evade host immunity by replicating within vertebrate erythrocytes.
source: Malaria parasites evade host immunity by replicating within vertebrate erythrocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum uses multiple ligands for erythrocyte invasion.
source: In humans, the virulent Plasmodium falciparum pathogen uses multiple ligands for erythrocyte invasion (Cowman et al., 2012) and then remodels its host cell to achieve tissue adherence and nutrient acquisition (Goldberg and Cowman, 2010; Wahlgren et al., 2017; Desai, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: P. falciparum remodels its host cell to achieve tissue adherence and nutrient acquisition.
source: In humans, the virulent Plasmodium falciparum pathogen uses multiple ligands for erythrocyte invasion (Cowman et al., 2012) and then remodels its host cell to achieve tissue adherence and nutrient acquisition (Goldberg and Cowman, 2010; Wahlgren et al., 2017; Desai, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: The RhopH complex contributes to erythrocyte invasion, tissue adherence, and nutrient acquisition despite their separate timings and cellular locations.
source: Remarkably, a single protein complex, termed RhopH, contributes to each of these activities despite their separate timings and cellular locations (Gupta et al., 2015; Goel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: The three subunits of the RhopH complex are CLAG, RhopH2, and RhopH3.
source: The three subunits of the RhopH complex, known as CLAG, RhopH2, and RhopH3, are conserved and restricted to Plasmodium spp.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The RhopH complex subunits are conserved and restricted to Plasmodium spp.
source: The three subunits of the RhopH complex, known as CLAG, RhopH2, and RhopH3, are conserved and restricted to Plasmodium spp.; none have significant homology to proteins in other genera (Kaneko, 2007), suggesting that these proteins and the complex they form evolved to meet the specific demands of bloodstream parasite survival.
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: RhopH complex subunits have no significant homology to proteins in other genera.
source: The three subunits of the RhopH complex, known as CLAG, RhopH2, and RhopH3, are conserved and restricted to Plasmodium spp.; none have significant homology to proteins in other genera (Kaneko, 2007), suggesting that these proteins and the complex they form evolved to meet the specific demands of bloodstream parasite survival.
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: RhopH2 and RhopH3 are single-copy genes in all Plasmodium spp.
source: While RhopH2 and RhopH3 are single-copy genes in all Plasmodium spp., CLAG proteins are encoded by a multigene family with variable expansion in malaria parasite species infecting humans and other vertebrates including birds, rodents, and primates (Kaneko et al., 2001; Cortés et al., 2007; Rovira-Graells et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: CLAG proteins are encoded by a multigene family with variable expansion in malaria parasite species.
source: While RhopH2 and RhopH3 are single-copy genes in all Plasmodium spp., CLAG proteins are encoded by a multigene family with variable expansion in malaria parasite species infecting humans and other vertebrates including birds, rodents, and primates (Kaneko et al., 2001; Cortés et al., 2007; Rovira-Graells et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: RhopH subunits are transcribed in mature schizont-infected erythrocytes.
source: Each of these subunits is transcribed in mature schizont-infected erythrocytes (Figure 1A; Ling et al., 2004); during translation, these proteins assemble with unknown stoichiometries into a complex that is packaged into rhoptry organelles (Ito et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: RhopH proteins assemble into a complex that is packaged into rhoptry organelles.
source: Each of these subunits is transcribed in mature schizont-infected erythrocytes (Figure 1A; Ling et al., 2004); during translation, these proteins assemble with unknown stoichiometries into a complex that is packaged into rhoptry organelles (Ito et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: RhopH3 facilitates invasion of erythrocytes.
source: Upon host cell rupture, RhopH3, but not CLAG or RhopH2 subunits, facilitates invasion of the next erythrocyte.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: CLAG3 inserts in the host erythrocyte membrane to form the plasmodial surface anion channel (PSAC) for nutrient uptake approximately 18 hours after invasion.
source: Some 18 hr later, CLAG3, a paralog encoded by the parasite chromosome 3, inserts in the host erythrocyte membrane to form the plasmodial surface anion channel (PSAC) for nutrient uptake (Desai et al., 2000; Nguitragool et al., 2011; Pillai et al., 2012); other paralogs may also contribute to PSAC (Gupta et al., 2020) or, in the case of CLAG9, to cytoadherence (Trenholme et al., 2000; Goel et al., 2010; Nacer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: RhopH2 and RhopH3 traffic to the host membrane and are required for PSAC activity.
source: RhopH2 and RhopH3 also traffic to the host membrane and are required for PSAC activity (Ito et al., 2017; Counihan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: Alkaline Na2CO3 extraction partially releases CLAG3 from infected cell membranes.
source: Alkaline Na2CO3 extraction but not hypotonic treatment partially released CLAG3 from infected cell membranes (Figure 1B, top row), implicating both integral and peripheral membrane pools.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hypotonic treatment does not release CLAG3 from infected cell membranes.
source: Alkaline Na2CO3 extraction but not hypotonic treatment partially released CLAG3 from infected cell membranes (Figure 1B, top row), implicating both integral and peripheral membrane pools.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Freeze-thaw releases CLAG3 from the peripheral membrane pool.
source: We found that simple freeze-thaw also releases some CLAG3 from the peripheral pool (bottom row); although Na2CO3 extraction releases a larger amount, freeze–thaw is gentler and does not denature many proteins.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Native mass spectrometry yielded a molecular weight of 433,790 ± 10 Da for the RhopH complex.
source: Native mass spectrometry (MS) yielded a molecular weight of 433,790 ± 10 Da (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), matching the expected mass for a heterotrimeric complex with a 1:1:1 stoichiometry; a 0.6% mass error may reflect post-translational modification and/or proteolytic processing, as reported for RhopH3 (Ito et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a primary finding from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A minor CLAG3–RhopH2 heterodimer with molecular weight 333,232 ± 3 Da was detected.
source: A smaller 333,232 ± 3 Da fraction corresponded to a minor CLAG3–RhopH2 heterodimer.
evidence: This is a finding from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: The purified RhopH complex resists aggregation and unfolding at temperatures above those seen in malaria fevers.
source: Finally, the purified RhopH complex resisted aggregation and unfolding at temperatures above those seen in malaria fevers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from thermal stability assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The RhopH complex has a two-lobed structure.
source: Three-dimensional reconstruction provided a low-resolution image of the entire complex and established a two-lobed structure (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Initial cryo-EM analyses yielded a two-lobed structure with a 3.3 Å resolution.
source: Initial analyses with 2D and 3D classifications yielded a two-lobed structure with a 3.3 Å resolution (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Table 1); per-particle contrast transfer function (CTF) estimation and motion correction improved overall resolution to 2.9 Å.
evidence: This is a finding from cryo-EM analysis detailed in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Per-particle CTF estimation and motion correction improved overall resolution to 2.9 Å.
source: Initial analyses with 2D and 3D classifications yielded a two-lobed structure with a 3.3 Å resolution (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Table 1); per-particle contrast transfer function (CTF) estimation and motion correction improved overall resolution to 2.9 Å.
evidence: This is a finding from cryo-EM data processing.

claim: CLAG3 mediates subunit associations through independent contacts with RhopH2 and RhopH3.
source: Soluble RhopH is a heterotrimeric complex consisting of single CLAG3, RhopH2, and RhopH3 subunits (Figure 2A), as predicted above. CLAG3 mediates subunit associations through independent contacts with RhopH2 and RhopH3, which do not directly interact with one another.
evidence: This is a finding from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: RhopH2 and RhopH3 do not directly interact with one another.
source: CLAG3 mediates subunit associations through independent contacts with RhopH2 and RhopH3, which do not directly interact with one another.
evidence: This is a finding from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: CLAG3 contains three visually distinct domains: an N-terminal sphere, an elongated central bridge for binding RhopH2, and a C-terminal bundle.
source: CLAG3 contains three visually distinct domains (Figure 2C): an N-terminal sphere, an elongated central bridge for binding RhopH2, and a C-terminal bundle encasing an amphipathic helix that later integrates in the host erythrocyte membrane (Sharma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The CLAG3 C-terminal bundle encases an amphipathic helix that later integrates in the host erythrocyte membrane.
source: CLAG3 contains three visually distinct domains (Figure 2C): an N-terminal sphere, an elongated central bridge for binding RhopH2, and a C-terminal bundle encasing an amphipathic helix that later integrates in the host erythrocyte membrane (Sharma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support and shown in the structure.

claim: The CLAG3 1300 loop and 300 region form orthogonal pincer-grasp interactions with RhopH3.
source: The N- and C-terminal domains hold RhopH3 tightly through bidentate interactions via a '1300 loop' and a '300 region' that form orthogonal pincer-grasp interactions.
evidence: This is a finding from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The CLAG3–RhopH3 interface is 3700 Å2.
source: Together, the 300 region and 1300 loop produce an extensive 3700 Å2 CLAG3 interface with RhopH3.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from structural analysis.

claim: The CLAG3–RhopH2 interface is 2005 Å2.
source: The 2005 Å2 CLAG3–RhopH2 interface is much more fragmented (residues 706–715, 787–805, and 920–939 of CLAG3 and 414–435, 580–594, 682–708, and 760 from RhopH2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from structural analysis.

claim: Each RhopH subunit has numerous conserved cysteines that contribute to tight assembly through disulfide bonds.
source: Each subunit has numerous conserved cysteines that contribute to tight assembly of this large complex through the formation of observed and possible disulfide bonds (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: No disulfide bonding between RhopH subunits was detected.
source: Although we did not detect bonding between subunits, several cysteines were not visualized and could form such interactions.
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis.

claim: P. falciparum CLAG paralogs cluster into well-supported groups containing species infecting other mammals.
source: We examined CLAG phylogeny and found that P. falciparum paralogs cluster into well-supported groups containing species infecting other mammals (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: CLAG9 represents an older lineage that clustered independently.
source: CLAG9 clustered independently and represented an older lineage.
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: RhopH3 exhibits structural similarity with domains from SepL, a regulator of type III translocon-based secretion in bacteria.
source: RhopH3 exhibited the greatest structural similarity with alignment to domains from SepL, a regulator of type III translocon-based secretion in bacteria (Burkinshaw et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from structural similarity searches with citation support.

claim: RhopH2 partially aligned with Bcl-xL, an anti-apoptotic protein that regulates membrane permeabilization.
source: RhopH2 partially aligned with Bcl-xL, an anti-apoptotic protein that also regulates membrane permeabilization (Finucane et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a finding from structural similarity searches with citation support.

claim: CLAG3 has a single confidently predicted transmembrane domain (α-helix 44).
source: Biochemical studies point to a direct contribution of the RhopH complex in PSAC-mediated nutrient uptake (Gupta et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2020), with a single confidently predicted CLAG3 transmembrane domain distal to a 10–30 residue hypervariable region (HVR, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated with citation support and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Site-directed mutagenesis of conserved A1215 residue in CLAG3 transmembrane domain alters channel gating, selectivity, and conductance.
source: Site-directed mutagenesis of a conserved A1215 residue in this transmembrane domain (α-helix 44 in our structure) alters channel gating, selectivity, and conductance, supporting a pore-lining helix (Sharma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: CLAG3 α-helix 44 and several neighboring helices align significantly with APH-1, an integral membrane component of human γ-secretase.
source: Notably, a PDB structure search identified this and several neighboring helices with a significant alignment to APH-1, an integral membrane component of human γ-secretase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from structural similarity searches shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CLAG3 α-helix 44 is buried within a CLAG3 C-terminal bundle.
source: This important helix is buried within a CLAG3 C-terminal bundle (Figure 3B–D), paralleling buried hydrophobic helices in some much smaller pore-forming proteins (Dal Peraro and van der Goot, 2016; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Multiple Phe side chains segregate to one surface of CLAG3 helix 44 and polar side chains line up at the opposite face.
source: Transverse and longitudinal views establish that multiple Phe side chains segregate to one surface of helix 44 and that polar side chains line up at the opposite face (Figure 3E), as expected for a helix that lines an aqueous pore (Sharma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CLAG3 helix 44 exhibits little primary sequence conservation despite conserved physicochemical properties.
source: Although its physicochemical properties are conserved in CLAG orthologs, helix 44 exhibits little primary sequence conservation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from conservation analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The CLAG3 hypervariable region (HVR) was poorly ordered in the structure.
source: In contrast to this helix, the nearby HVR was poorly ordered, consistent with an unstructured extracellular loop that functions as an immune decoy (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The single predicted transmembrane domains on RhopH2 and RhopH3 are buried in the soluble structure.
source: The single predicted transmembrane domains on RhopH2 and RhopH3 are also buried in the soluble structure (helices defined by V740-D757 and G595-Y622 of these subunits, respectively; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: During stage-specific synthesis in schizont-infected cells, both peripheral and integral membrane pools of RhopH were reproducibly detected.
source: During stage-specific synthesis in schizont-infected cells (Ling et al., 2004), both peripheral and integral membrane pools were reproducibly detected (Figure 4A, top row).
evidence: This is a finding from fractionation studies shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The integral CLAG3 pool in early schizont-stage cultures was quantitatively proteolyzed by extracellular protease treatment.
source: As the integral pool was quantitatively proteolyzed (Figure 4A,B), we conclude that the integral pool in these cells reflects protein made in the previous cycle; the larger carbonate-extractable pool represents newly synthesized protein.
evidence: This is a finding from protease susceptibility studies shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Purified merozoites contain carbonate-extractable CLAG3 and undetectable levels of integral protein.
source: Fractionation studies using purified merozoites revealed carbonate-extractable CLAG3 and undetectable levels of integral protein (Figure 4C), consistent with packaging of newly synthesized RhopH complex into rhoptries and jettisoning of the prior-cycle integral host membrane pool upon schizont rupture; the host membrane marker, Band3, is also discarded at egress.
evidence: This is a finding from fractionation studies shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Merozoites transfer their peripheral CLAG3 pool to immature ring-stage parasites.
source: We then tracked this newly synthesized pool through the parasite bloodstream cycle and found that merozoites transfer their peripheral CLAG3 pool to immature ring-stage parasites, which also carry negligible amounts of the integral form (Figure 4D,E, rings).
evidence: This is a finding from stage-dependent fractionation studies shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: CLAG3 transitions from a primarily extractable form in schizonts into a growing integral pool in trophozoites.
source: With parasite maturation, CLAG3 transitions from a primarily extractable form upon synthesis in schizonts into a growing integral pool after transfer into new erythrocytes (Figure 4D,E, trophozoites).
evidence: This is a finding from stage-dependent fractionation studies shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: CLAG3 remains associated with other RhopH subunits during conversion to integral form.
source: During this conversion, CLAG3 remains associated with other RhopH subunits and eventually localizes to the infected host cell membrane (Vincensini et al., 2008; Nguitragool et al., 2011; Ahmad et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: PTEX knockdown abolishes CLAG3 transition to an integral form.
source: We found that CLAG3 transitions to an integral form in this parasite normally in the presence of TMP, but that PTEX knockdown produces a loss of integral CLAG3 (-TMP, p = 0.01, n = 3).
evidence: This is a finding from PTEX knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claim: CLAG3 that failed to insert into the membrane was more readily solubilized in PTEX knockdown parasites.
source: CLAG3 that failed to insert into the membrane was more readily solubilized (-TMP, soluble lane), possibly due to protein crowding as a result of blocked export from the parasitophorous vacuole.
evidence: This is a finding from PTEX knockdown experiments with speculation about mechanism.

claim: Both the freeze–thaw released and carbonate-extractable pools of CLAG3 were unaffected by extracellular protease.
source: Both the freeze–thaw released and carbonate-extractable pools of CLAG3 were unaffected by extracellular protease, but the integral pool at the host membrane yielded a C-terminal cleavage product that remained membrane embedded (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from protease susceptibility studies shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The integral CLAG3 pool at the host membrane yielded a C-terminal cleavage product that remained membrane embedded upon protease treatment.
source: Both the freeze–thaw released and carbonate-extractable pools of CLAG3 were unaffected by extracellular protease, but the integral pool at the host membrane yielded a C-terminal cleavage product that remained membrane embedded (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from protease susceptibility studies shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CLAG3 α-helix 44 is within the protease-resistant cleavage fragment and likely provides the transmembrane anchor.
source: α-Helix 44 is within this cleavage fragment and likely provides the responsible transmembrane anchor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the protease susceptibility data.

claim: RhopH evolved as a modular three-protein complex suited for essential and divergent functions at separate points in the bloodstream parasite cycle.
source: We propose that RhopH evolved as a modular three-protein complex suited for essential and divergent functions at separate points in the bloodstream parasite cycle (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings of the study, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: A soluble form of RhopH, packaged into rhoptry secretory organelles, facilitates RhopH3 contribution to erythrocyte invasion.
source: A soluble form, packaged into rhoptry secretory organelles, facilitates RhopH3 contribution to erythrocyte invasion through still unknown mechanisms that presumably involve surface interactions.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings of the study.

claim: RhopH3 has a large exposed surface area of ~32,000 Å2.
source: A large exposed surface area of ~32,000 Å2 and globular architecture of RhopH3 provide candidates for inquiry.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from structural analysis.

claim: RhopH3 residues 434–665 align with domains 2 and 3 of SepL.
source: Our structure similarity searches found that RhopH3 residues 434–665 align with domains 2 and 3 of SepL; because domain three mediates interaction with the Tir receptor (Burkinshaw et al., 2015), one possibility is that RhopH3 interacts with an unidentified host cell receptor at this site.
evidence: This is a finding from structural similarity searches with speculation about function.

claim: The RhopH3 C-terminus (residues 716–897) is not resolved in the structure and appears to be flexible.
source: This entire region (residues 716–897) is not resolved in our structure and appears to be flexible.
evidence: This is a finding from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The soluble RhopH complex crosses the parasitophorous vacuolar membrane and is deposited in the parasitophorous vacuole in a soluble form.
source: A soluble RhopH complex may also facilitate transfer to new erythrocytes for a second role in PSAC-mediated nutrient uptake (Nguitragool et al., 2011). We determined that the complex is transferred to the new host cell and deposited in the parasitophorous vacuole in a soluble form.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: RhopH subunits may be exported into host cell cytosol via PTEX.
source: The member subunits may then be exported into host cell cytosol via PTEX, as suggested by confocal immunofluorescence assays showing blocked export of each RhopH subunit in PTEX knockdown parasites (Ito et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as a possibility.

claim: The RhopH complex directly interacts with PTEX to enter host cell cytosol.
source: Forward and reverse coimmunoprecipitation experiments also suggest that the RhopH complex directly interacts with PTEX to enter host cell cytosol (de Koning-Ward et al., 2009; Counihan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as a suggestion.

claim: PTEX appears to lack a lateral gate used by other translocons to transfer cargo proteins into the adjacent lipid bilayer.
source: Although membrane insertion during transit through PTEX would follow the precedent of Sec translocon-mediated membrane insertion in bacteria and other eukaryotes (Denks et al., 2014), PTEX appears to lack a lateral gate, as used by other translocons to transfer cargo proteins into the adjacent lipid bilayer (Egea and Stroud, 2010; Corey et al., 2019; Ho et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Membrane insertion of RhopH may occur after transfer into host cytosol.
source: We tend to favor membrane insertion after transfer into host cytosol.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors.

claim: Various studies support a role of the RhopH complex in PSAC formation and nutrient uptake.
source: Although various studies support a role of the RhopH complex in PSAC formation and nutrient uptake (Nguitragool et al., 2011; Mira-Martínez et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2013; Ito et al., 2017; Counihan et al., 2017), whether this ternary complex directly forms the aqueous pore in the host erythrocyte membrane remains debated.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: In vitro selection implicated a short amphipathic CLAG3 motif in solute selectivity and PSAC single-channel gating.
source: In vitro selection previously implicated a short, but critical amphipathic CLAG3 motif in solute selectivity and PSAC single-channel gating (Lisk et al., 2008; Sharma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: CLAG3 oligomerizes at the host membrane.
source: While studies suggest that CLAG3 oligomerizes at the host membrane and has an surface-exposed variant region (Figure 5; Gupta et al., 2018; Nguitragool et al., 2014), RhopH2 and RhopH3 are not exposed based on protease susceptibility studies (Ito et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: RhopH2 and RhopH3 are not exposed at the host membrane based on protease susceptibility studies.
source: While studies suggest that CLAG3 oligomerizes at the host membrane and has an surface-exposed variant region (Figure 5; Gupta et al., 2018; Nguitragool et al., 2014), RhopH2 and RhopH3 are not exposed based on protease susceptibility studies (Ito et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The three predicted transmembrane helices on CLAG3, RhopH2, and RhopH3 are separated from one another by 46–101 Å in the soluble structure.
source: The CLAG3 helix 44 and the individual predicted transmembrane domains on RhopH2 and RhopH3 are separated from one another by 46–101 Å in the soluble structure (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from structural analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: If all three transmembrane helices come together to form the eventual nutrient pore, a remarkable rearrangement of the complex will be required.
source: If all three helices come together to form the eventual nutrient pore, a remarkable rearrangement of the complex will be required during its conversion from a soluble to a membrane-inserted form.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural findings.
